content: 1. The quality of evidence is categorized as high, moderate, low, or very low. Specific populations at higher risk for hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection include people who inject drugs (PWID), individuals in prisons or other closed settings, men who have sex with men (MSM), sex workers, HIV-infected persons, and children born to mothers with chronic HCV infection, particularly if the mothers are co-infected with HIV. 2. Clinical features that may suggest underlying chronic HCV infection include evidence of existing liver disease, such as cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Unexplained liver disease, including abnormal liver function tests or findings on liver ultrasound, may also indicate chronic HCV infection. 3. A seroprevalence threshold of ≥2% or ≥5% is used to define intermediate and high prevalence, respectively. The choice of threshold depends on country-specific considerations and the epidemiological context. 4. Routine testing for HCV infection in pregnant women is not currently recommended. 5. Historical exposure to unscreened or inadequately screened blood products and/or unsafe injection practices has contributed to the spread of HCV. 6. Abbreviations used include ALT (alanine aminotransferase), AST (aspartate aminotransferase), APRI (aspartate-to-platelet ratio index), HBeAg (hepatitis B e antigen), HBsAg (hepatitis B surface antigen), NAT (nucleic acid test), and RDT (rapid diagnostic test). 7. A complete vaccination schedule, including a birth dose, should be administered to all infants in accordance with the World Health Organization (WHO) position paper on hepatitis B vaccines (2009). Testing exposed infants for HBsAg between 6 and 12 months of age is recommended to screen for hepatitis B infection, as serological testing before 6 months may yield inconsistent results due to the presence of maternal antibodies. 8. Acute hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection can be confirmed by detecting HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc. Chronic HBV infection is diagnosed when HBsAg persists for six months or more. 9. Laboratory-based immunoassays for HBV diagnosis include enzyme immunoassay (EIA), chemiluminescence immunoassay (CLIA), and electrochemiluminescence assay (ECL). These assays should meet minimum quality and performance standards, such as WHO prequalification or stringent regulatory review. 10. For chronic HBV infection, a single serological assay to detect HBsAg is recommended as the initial diagnostic step. In settings with limited laboratory access, rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are recommended to improve access to care and treatment. 11. Following a positive HBsAg test, quantitative or qualitative nucleic acid testing (NAT) for HBV DNA is recommended to guide treatment decisions. Monitoring for treatment response and disease progression should include annual assessments of ALT, HBsAg, HBeAg, and HBV DNA levels, as well as non-invasive tests like APRI or transient elastography to evaluate liver fibrosis or cirrhosis. 12. More frequent monitoring (every three months during the first year) is recommended for individuals with advanced liver disease, those on treatment, or those who have discontinued treatment. This is particularly important for individuals with fluctuating ALT or HBV DNA levels, HIV co-infection, or adherence concerns. 13. Chronic HCV infection in children under 18 months can only be confirmed using virological assays to detect HCV RNA, as maternal antibodies may persist in the child’s bloodstream until 18 months of age, making serological test results ambiguous. 14. For HCV diagnosis, a single serological assay to detect antibodies or antigens is recommended as the initial step, followed by NAT to confirm viraemic infection. In settings with limited laboratory infrastructure, RDTs are recommended to facilitate linkage to care. 15. Sustained virological response (SVR12 or SVR24) after antiviral treatment completion is used to confirm the absence of active HCV infection. 16. Decompensated cirrhosis is defined by the development of complications such as portal hypertension (ascites, variceal hemorrhage, hepatic encephalopathy), coagulopathy, or liver insufficiency (jaundice). 17. The APRI score is a simple index for estimating hepatic fibrosis, calculated using the formula: APRI = [(AST/AST ULN) x 100] / platelet count (10^9/L). A value of 40 IU/L is commonly used as the upper limit of normal (ULN) for AST. 18. Transient elastography (FibroScan) is a non-invasive technique to measure liver stiffness as a surrogate for fibrosis. 19. ALT levels in individuals with chronic hepatitis B may fluctuate and require longitudinal monitoring to determine trends. Persistently abnormal ALT levels may warrant treatment, but other causes of elevated ALT, such as impaired glucose tolerance, dyslipidemia, or fatty liver, should be excluded. 20. Strategies to improve uptake of hepatitis testing and linkage to care include peer and lay health worker support in community-based settings and clinician reminders in facilities with electronic records. These interventions aim to enhance testing and treatment initiation, particularly in high-risk populations such as those in drug treatment programs or prisons.
